options_ranked.title: Base Oil Procurement Forensic Audit & Forward Hedging Lock-In
options_ranked.description: A 10-day forensic review of base oil supplier invoices, spot-market pricing, and hedging positions for YTD purchases to determine whether COGS reflects spot spikes or contract repricing, followed immediately by forward procurement locks (3–6 month fixed-price agreements or futures) at current market levels. This stops further margin bleed on the confirmed COGS-driven mechanism and builds the documented cost baseline needed to justify recovery pricing at renewal. Scope note: targets the four compressed oil SKUs (Synthetic Blend -7.14, Conventional -6.61, Compressor -5.86, Hydraulic -5.76); periods within threshold and unaffected segments need no action.
options_ranked.rationale: The only confirmed causal chain in the verified model runs from base oil, manufacturing, distribution, and packaging costs into COGS and thence into Gross Margin %. Four products compressing 5.8–7.1 points in parallel is the signature of a shared input-cost shock, not four independent commercial problems. With list prices locked, the supply side is where the recovery lives — and the audit distinguishes a real cost shock from a costing-methodology artefact before any money is committed.
options_ranked.time_to_value: 10 days to diagnosis; 30–90 days to hedged cost stabilization

arguments_for: Directly targets the confirmed COGS-to-margin mechanism — the only client-validated causal path — rather than betting on an unconfirmed mix prior.
The audit is falsifiable within 10 days: invoices either show base oil unit-cost inflation matching the compression or they do not, cheaply redirecting effort if the diagnosis is wrong.
arguments_against: Hedging at current levels locks in an elevated cost floor; if base oil spot prices subsequently fall, the business forgoes that relief.
Cost containment alone cannot restore the full 7.14-point gap while the price-lock prevents any revenue-side offset until renewal.
key_questions: What percentage of Synthetic Blend COGS is base oil, and how did that unit cost move YTD versus published benchmarks?
What hedging instruments and counterparty limits are available within existing treasury policy?

implementation_triggers: Audit confirms base oil unit-cost inflation explains a majority of the compression
Base oil forward curve is flat or rising, making a lock-in favorable
prerequisites: Access to supplier invoice detail and YTD procurement records for base oil
Treasury approval framework for forward purchase or futures instruments
Baseline unit-cost bridge for Synthetic Blend and Conventional Engine Oil

impact_estimate.basis: If base oil inflation accounts for 60–75% of Synthetic Blend Engine Oil's 7.14-point compression, hedging plus procurement optimization recovers 4.2–6.8 points on that segment by Q3; this range sizes the driving segment, not the 4.49-pt enterprise headline.

key_assumptions.assumption: Base oil cost inflation accounts for 60–75% of the observed compression in the affected SKUs.
key_assumptions.provenance: The 10-day invoice audit showing base oil unit cost up 8–12% YTD would be consistent with this; flat base oil costs would falsify it and redirect attention to distribution or manufacturing lines.

key_assumptions.assumption: COGS movements directly drive Gross Margin % with revenue held constant.
key_assumptions.provenance: Client-confirmed direct relationship: gross_margin_pct <-> cogs, plus confirmed base_oil_cost -> COGS component summation.

key_assumptions.assumption: Forward locks at current market levels prevent further deterioration rather than crystallizing a peak price.
key_assumptions.provenance: Base oil spot price staying at or above the lock level for two consecutive periods would confirm; a sustained fall below it would falsify.

options_ranked.title: Mix Acceleration into Premium Formulations + Renewal-Window Contract Repricing
options_ranked.description: Redirect sales incentives and channel promotion away from the degraded Value-tier SKUs (Synthetic Blend at 20.64%, Conventional at 19.16%) toward High Mileage and Full Synthetic variants, while preparing cost-escalation contract language (indexed to published base oil benchmarks) for anchor accounts strictly at their next renewal window. No repricing action touches any anchor account mid-quarter. Scope note: only the Value category and the four degraded oil SKUs are targeted; timeframe buckets outside the YTD window are within threshold and require no intervention. Consistency caveat: the assumption that premium variants out-margin Synthetic Blend rests on an unconfirmed prior — Step 1 is a margin verification of the target SKUs before incentives shift volume toward them.
options_ranked.rationale: This is a demand-side path to margin recovery that fully respects the price-lock constraint by deferring all repricing to contractual renewal windows. It converts the current cost shock into renewal leverage: a documented cost baseline plus indexation language prevents recurrence. The mix contribution is deliberately capped in the estimate (0.85–1.4 pp) because the premium-mix-to-margin relationship is an unconfirmed prior and input-cost pressure could mask the mix benefit.
options_ranked.time_to_value: 30–90 days for mix effects; renewal-cycle timing for repricing

arguments_for: Improves blended margin without touching locked list prices, making it the only revenue-side lever legally available this quarter.
Renewal-window indexation permanently transfers future base oil inflation risk to customers, preventing a repeat of the unrecovered cost pass-through.
arguments_against: The margin advantage of premium variants is assumed from positioning, not verified — if premium SKUs are also cost-compressed, the mix shift delivers little.
If input-cost inflation dominates, margin can keep falling even as premium mix rises, meaning mix alone cannot close the 7.14-point gap.
key_questions: What are the current verified gross margins of High Mileage and Full Synthetic YTD, and did they also compress?
Which anchor accounts reach renewal within the next two quarters, and what volume do they represent?

implementation_triggers: Verified premium-SKU margins exceed Synthetic Blend by at least 4 points
prerequisites: SKU-level margin verification for High Mileage and Full Synthetic before incentive redesign
Legal review confirming no renewal-preparation activity constitutes effective mid-quarter repricing of locked accounts
Channel capacity check that premium volume can be absorbed without discounting

impact_estimate.basis: A 15–20 pp mix shift from Synthetic Blend (20.64% margin) toward premium variants recovers roughly 0.85–1.4 pp of blended margin, with the balance (2.0–2.8 pp) positioned at contract renewal via indexed cost pass-through — sized against the 4.49-pt headline decline.

key_assumptions.assumption: High Mileage and Full Synthetic carry structurally higher gross margin than Synthetic Blend and were not equally compressed by the cost shock.
key_assumptions.provenance: SKU-level YTD margin report showing premium variants at or above ~26% margin would confirm; parallel compression in premium SKUs would falsify.

key_assumptions.assumption: Anchor accounts will accept indexed cost-escalation clauses at renewal in exchange for volume commitments.
key_assumptions.provenance: First two renewal negotiations closing with indexation language intact would confirm; rejection or churn would falsify.

key_assumptions.assumption: Sales incentives can shift 15–20 pp of volume mix within 90 days.
key_assumptions.provenance: Monthly premium mix share moving at least 5 pp within 60 days of incentive launch would confirm.

flagged_side_effects: The mix-to-margin mechanism rests on an unconfirmed industry prior: margin can fall even while premium mix rises if input-cost pressure dominates, so mix shift alone may not close the 7.14-point gap — the estimate caps the mix contribution accordingly and requires premium-margin verification as a prerequisite.

Any renegotiation activity ahead of renewal risks conflicting with the mid-quarter price-lock clause — an explicit guardrail restricts all repricing to contractual renewal windows, with legal sign-off before any anchor account is contacted.

options_ranked.title: COGS Component Waterfall & Value-Tier Portfolio Reallocation Decision
options_ranked.description: A 30-day cost-component decomposition of COGS for Synthetic Blend and Conventional Engine Oil across base oil, distribution, manufacturing, and packaging accounts, feeding an explicit portfolio decision: (a) accept structurally lower Value-tier margins and reallocate emphasis to higher-resilience SKUs, (b) renegotiate supplier and freight contracts, or (c) de-emphasize or exit the most-pressured SKU next quarter. Consistency caveat: before reallocating volume toward premium SKUs, this option requires verification that those targets were NOT equally compressed — if they were, the resolution path is supplier renegotiation first, reallocation second. Scope note: decision applies to the Value category (-6.42) and the four degraded oil SKUs only.
options_ranked.rationale: This option questions the frame the other two optimize inside: if the cost inflation is structural and durable (commodity regime shift rather than a spike), then hedging and mix incentives only delay a participation decision on the Value tier. The waterfall classifies the shock as structural, contractual, or operational, and each classification maps to a different — and materially different-cost — response, preventing the business from spending recovery effort on a category that no longer earns its capital.
options_ranked.time_to_value: 30 days to decomposition; 3–12 months for reallocation economics to land

arguments_for: Prevents committing hedging capital and sales incentives to a Value tier whose margin decline may be structural category deterioration rather than a fixable variance.
All four COGS components it decomposes are client-confirmed drivers, so the diagnostic itself rests entirely on validated relationships.
arguments_against: De-emphasis or exit is largely irreversible and forfeits volume-based leverage in the very anchor-account renewals the other options depend on.
A structural response to what may be a one-time spot spike would over-solve the problem at high cost — the shock's durability is not yet established.
key_questions: Do base oil forward curves indicate a durable price regime shift or a transient spike?
What fixed-cost absorption and customer-relationship consequences follow from de-emphasizing Value-tier volume?

implementation_triggers: Waterfall shows the dominant cost driver is structural commodity inflation not addressable by negotiation
Two consecutive quarters of Value-tier margin below the portfolio cost-of-capital hurdle
prerequisites: Completed COGS component decomposition (can reuse the procurement audit's invoice work)
Verified margin comparison between reallocation-target SKUs and the Value tier
Exit-economics model covering fixed-cost absorption, anchor-account contract exposure, and channel commitments

impact_estimate.basis: Assumes cost isolation identifies 35–50% of the 7.14-point Synthetic Blend compression as addressable via supplier negotiation or SKU reallocation; range sized against the 4.49-pt enterprise headline decline and sits at its ceiling.

key_assumptions.assumption: The margin compression is structural and durable rather than a transient spot-price spike.
key_assumptions.provenance: Base oil benchmark prices remaining elevated for two further quarters would be consistent with this; reversion to prior-year levels would falsify it.

key_assumptions.assumption: Reallocation-target SKUs retain materially better margin resilience than the Value tier.
key_assumptions.provenance: SKU-level YTD margin deltas showing target SKUs compressed by less than 2 points versus the Value tier's 6.42 would confirm.

key_assumptions.assumption: The four confirmed COGS components (base oil, distribution, manufacturing, packaging) fully account for the compression.
key_assumptions.provenance: Client-confirmed account_category summation of these components into COGS; a residual unexplained after decomposition would indicate a costing-allocation artefact instead.

flagged_side_effects: Portfolio de-emphasis or exit decisions are hard to reverse and could weaken volume leverage in anchor-account renewal negotiations that the mix-and-repricing path relies on.

solutions.recommendation_rationale: The parallel compression across Synthetic Blend (-7.14), Conventional (-6.61), Compressor (-5.86) and Hydraulic Oil (-5.76) is the signature of a shared input-cost shock, and the only client-confirmed causal path to Gross Margin % runs through COGS and its base oil, distribution, manufacturing, and packaging components. The 10-day procurement audit and hedging lock-in acts directly on that confirmed mechanism, is falsifiable within days, respects the mid-quarter price-lock clause, and produces the documented cost baseline that both the renewal-window repricing play and the portfolio reallocation decision require as an input — making it the correct first move regardless of which longer play follows.

problem_reframe.situation: Gross Margin % has dropped by 7.14 points year-to-date at the driving segment (Synthetic Blend Engine Oil, now 20.64% vs 27.78% prior), with the overall portfolio margin down 4.49 points (29.94% vs 34.43% prior year-to-date).
problem_reframe.complication: Compression is broad but uneven: Synthetic Blend (-7.14), Conventional Engine Oil (-6.61), Compressor Oil (-5.86), Hydraulic Oil (-5.76) and the Value category (-6.42) are all degraded in parallel — a pattern consistent with a shared COGS-side driver — while timeframe buckets outside the YTD window remain within threshold, and a contractual price-lock clause on Lubricants anchor accounts blocks any mid-quarter list-price recovery.
problem_reframe.question: Which combination of cost-side containment, mix acceleration, and portfolio decisioning restores Gross Margin % toward its prior ~34% level fastest without violating the anchor-account price-lock?
key_assumptions: The parallel margin compression across four oil products reflects a common input-cost driver (base oil / distribution / manufacturing) rather than independent product-level demand shocks.
The price-lock clause holds through the current quarter, so near-term recovery must come from COGS or mix, not list price.
Premium formulations (High Mileage, Full Synthetic) still carry structurally higher margin than the degraded Value-tier SKUs — this rests on an unconfirmed industry prior, not validated data.

unresolved_tensions.tension: Hedging locks in current elevated base oil costs, while the portfolio path bets the inflation may be a transient spike — locking in a peak would crystallize the loss the reallocation view says to wait out.
unresolved_tensions.requires: Head of Procurement to deliver a base oil forward-curve assessment (spike vs regime shift) alongside the invoice audit before any hedge exceeding 3 months is executed (target: Day 10).

unresolved_tensions.tension: The mix-acceleration play shifts incentives toward premium SKUs whose superior margin is an unconfirmed prior, and the portfolio play may de-emphasize the same Value-tier volume that provides anchor-account renewal leverage.
unresolved_tensions.requires: FP&A lead to produce a verified SKU-level YTD margin bridge for High Mileage and Full Synthetic versus Synthetic Blend before sales incentives are redesigned (target: Week 2).

blind_spots: No customer- or channel-level margin data was surfaced — the compression could be concentrated in a few anchor accounts (discounting or rebate leakage) rather than being purely a COGS phenomenon.

The possibility that part of the measured decline is a costing-methodology artefact (allocation change, standard-cost revision) has not been ruled out; the audit must check measurement integrity before treating the full 7.14 points as economic.
Competitor pricing behavior is unobserved — if competitors are absorbing the same input inflation, renewal-window price recovery may cost share.
Demand elasticity of the Value tier is unknown, so the volume consequence of any renewal-cycle price increase is unquantified.
next_steps: Head of Procurement to complete the 10-day forensic audit of base oil supplier invoices, spot benchmarks, and hedging positions, delivering a unit-cost bridge for Synthetic Blend and Conventional Engine Oil (by Day 10).
CFO to approve treasury framework and counterparty limits for 3–6 month base oil forward locks, conditional on the audit confirming input-cost inflation as the dominant driver (by end of Week 2).
FP&A lead to deliver verified YTD gross margins for High Mileage and Full Synthetic versus the compressed Value-tier SKUs, gating any sales-incentive redesign (by end of Week 2).

General Counsel to map anchor-account renewal windows and draft indexed cost-escalation contract language, with an explicit guardrail that no locked account is approached mid-quarter (by end of Week 4).
VP Strategy to run the COGS component waterfall and present the Value-tier participation decision (retain/renegotiate/de-emphasize) with exit-economics modeling (by Day 30).

commercial.framework: Price-Volume-Mix Decomposition with Customer Profitability Analysis
commercial.hypothesis: Gross margin compression of 7.14 pp on Synthetic Blend Engine Oil is driven primarily by unrecovered input cost inflation (base oil and/or manufacturing costs) combined with contractual pricing rigidity on anchor accounts. The Value category decline (-6.42 pp) suggests margin pressure is concentrated in lower-tier SKUs where price-lock clauses prevent mid-quarter indexation, while COGS (base oil, manufacturing, distribution) has risen materially YTD without corresponding revenue recovery.
key_evidence: Synthetic Blend Engine Oil margin fell 7.14 pp (27.78% → 20.64%) YTD, the largest single-product deterioration, signaling product-specific cost or pricing stress rather than portfolio-wide demand shift.

Conventional Engine Oil declined 6.61 pp (25.77% → 19.16%), and both products sit in the Value category which fell 6.42 pp, indicating concentrated margin loss in price-sensitive, contractually locked tiers.

Confirmed COGS relationship shows base_oil_cost, manufacturing_cost, and distribution_cost sum directly into COGS; combined inflation across these three line items without pricing pass-through explains the magnitude of observed margin erosion.

operational.framework: Cost-to-Serve Analysis with Input-Cost Hedging Diagnostics
operational.hypothesis: Gross margin compression of 7.14 percentage points in Synthetic Blend Engine Oil is driven primarily by unhedged base oil cost inflation, not revenue price/mix deterioration. The -7.14 delta in the highest-margin synthetic product, coupled with parallel -6.61 delta in conventional oil and -5.86 in compressor oil, indicates a supply-side cost shock concentrated in base oil inputs. The constraint preventing mid-quarter price adjustments masks this cost pass-through, creating a temporary margin valley until contract renewal or procurement hedging takes effect.

proposed_option.description: Conduct a 30-day cost-component decomposition of COGS for Synthetic Blend and Conventional Engine Oil to isolate whether margin loss is driven by base oil price escalation, freight/distribution inflation, or manufacturing/packaging cost creep. Use findings to decide between: (a) accepting lower margin in Value/Conventional tier and reallocating portfolio emphasis to higher-resilience SKUs, or (b) negotiating supplier contracts for base oil and freight, or (c) exiting or de-emphasizing the most-pressured SKU within the next quarter.
proposed_option.mechanism: The hypothesis rests on COGS movement (confirmed direct relationship), not revenue decline. Decomposing COGS into base_oil_cost, distribution_cost, manufacturing_cost, and packaging_cost (all confirmed INDIRECT drivers via COGS) will identify which cost account is inflating. This isolates whether the margin loss is: (1) structural/durable (commodity input inflation → portfolio reallocation needed), (2) tactical/contractual (freight spike → negotiable), or (3) operational (manufacturing inefficiency → process fix). The constraint against mid-quarter price increases means revenue-side recovery is unavailable; cost isolation is the only frame-respecting lever.

impact_estimate.basis: Partial recovery assumes cost isolation identifies 35–50% of the 7.14-point compression as addressable via supplier negotiation or SKU reallocation (e.g., shifting volume mix toward higher-resilience products or renegotiating base oil contracts). Full recovery (7.14 points) is unlikely within 90 days given commodity dynamics and contractual constraints; realistic recovery targets 2.5–4.5 points through tactical cost management and portfolio shift.
